title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Maritime
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Officials weigh Iran’s role in up to 50 tanker cyberattacks as Coast Guard cyber teams board US-bound energy and chemical ships
items.content_text: US officials told the Wall Street Journal, in a report carried on 23–24 November, that Iran is the main suspect in as many as 50 cyberattacks on tankers carrying oil, gas and chemicals; Russia is also being examined, and an administration official says there is no evidence of Iranian involvement. The report widens a case made public in September, when the Coast Guard and FBI confirmed boarding two foreign-flagged, US-bound tankers in August after signs of network compromise. Cyber teams have since assisted at least four US-bound vessels, including the VL Prosperity, which received a ransom note and a bomb threat. Bloomberg reports that hackers reached one supertanker’s propulsion system, which is not confirmed, and no ship is reported disabled. Editorial assessment: shipboard firewalls and shore-to-ship remote access are now front-line targets.

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority knocks out access-control and port-coordination systems, forcing contingency procedures at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Santos Port Authority (APS), the state company that runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on the morning of 6 November, the same day a power cut hit its servers, and on 10 November confirmed a cyberattack. Platforms for physical access control, cargo handling and port-operations coordination were affected, and some services moved to email and manual checks, slowing some procedures. São Paulo’s port security commission raised the port’s protection level to 2 of 3 on 8 November. By 16 November core systems were in final tests; ship movements and land access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. Editorial assessment: gate access and berth coordination need a drilled manual fallback that does not depend on port-authority IT.

items.title: Maersk confirms data was stolen from a legacy system it inherited, as the WhiteArmor ransomware group demands $5 million
items.content_text: Maersk confirmed on 11 November that an attacker extracted data from one IT system it inherited through an acquisition, after the WhiteArmor ransomware group listed the company on its leak site on 7 November and demanded $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. WhiteArmor claims about 100 GB from a logistics platform linked to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought in 2022, including about 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords and mobile-device logs; those claims are unverified. Maersk says the incident is isolated to a local system, that its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data was disclosed, and that other Maersk systems and partner API and EDI connections show no impact. It has not said how or when the attacker got in. Editorial assessment: acquired platforms that were never fully integrated are a standing blind spot.

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 European countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost. Sweden’s NCSC says victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer with weak passwords, and Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. Belgium says its evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution (see the Iran card above). No port or vessel victim is reported. Editorial assessment: reefer yards and port cold stores with web-managed controllers should treat any internet-reachable unit as at risk.

items.title: Norway says the Equinor and Skagerak Energi intrusions came through Microsoft’s Azure API Management cloud service
items.content_text: On 23 November Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unidentified actor has been stealing access tokens and other sensitive data from Microsoft Azure API Management (APIM), and that Equinor and utility Skagerak Energi were among those hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it by 20 November; Skagerak disclosed a separate attack a day later. Both say production and operations carried on normally, and Equinor sees no sign data was stolen or altered. A reported, non-public Microsoft notice says an issue in older “Classic” APIM tiers was closed on 19 November; Microsoft has not publicly linked it to Norway. Editorial assessment: terminal and fleet operators using cloud APIs for cargo, vessel or plant data should rotate those secrets now.

items.title: n0n published data it says came from 38 port, shipping and logistics firms; none has confirmed a breach, and a shared software vendor is suspected
items.content_text: The data-theft extortion group n0n listed 38 maritime and logistics organizations in 18 countries on 12 October, including Ocean Network Express, Santos Brasil, TTI Algeciras and Eurogate Tanger, and claims EDI messages, manifests, vessel schedules, gate movements and terminal configuration records. SOCRadar and The Register reported on 28 and 30 October that all listings were published after the 19 October deadline, with no payments seen; the contents have not been independently analysed and no listed firm has confirmed a breach. Researchers link at least 21 of the 38 to customers of the South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, which has not confirmed an incident; the link is unverified. SOCRadar found that the break-ins it could document relied on weak or stolen credentials, not exploits. No operational disruption is reported.

items.title: China’s Volt Typhoon used throwaway relay chains to reach management and SD-WAN platforms at critical-infrastructure targets, maritime among them, Lumen says
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October on “Silent Train”, the covert access framework it says the China state-sponsored group Volt Typhoon has used since November 2023: each session runs through a short-lived chain of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment, built for one target and then discarded. Lumen says the aim is to gain and keep access to management and control-plane technology, and cites zero-day campaigns against N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875, CVE-2025-8876), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127) and VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), all in CISA’s KEV catalog. It lists maritime among the critical-infrastructure sectors with victims but names none, gives no count by sector and describes no OT access or operational impact. Editorial assessment: in port and ship-management networks, the SD-WAN orchestrator or remote-management server that can reconfigure every site deserves the same protection as the OT behind it.

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, water, energy and other sectors increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, while warning that weak systems could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing officials said they found no evidence that hackers caused the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent outages. For port and vessel operators, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while brands claiming industrial victims rose from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105). Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Editorial assessment: Dragos does not break out maritime, but carriers and terminals share the same IT-layer dependency.

items.title: GreyNoise says an AI-assisted crew breached Check Point firewall-management servers at 22 organizations, transport firms among them
items.content_text: GreyNoise reported on 24 November a campaign it tracks as GT13 that compromised Check Point Security Management servers at at least 22 organizations in several countries between 17 October and 2 November, and believes attempts continue. Victims include transportation, energy, mining, engineering and manufacturing firms; no port or shipping company is named. The attackers relayed through a Rejetto HFS file server, then used CVE-2026-16232 in SmartConsole to run scripts on management servers, copying firewall databases and internal certificate authorities and unloading security policies. GreyNoise believes AI tools did much of the work and cannot name the group; Check Point says no new vulnerability or technique is involved. Editorial assessment: a firewall manager holds the rules separating terminal OT and ship-shore links from business IT, so a stolen policy database is a map of that perimeter.

items.title: Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks: four of five succeeded, with critical-infrastructure operators among the targets
items.content_text: Switzerland’s Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on 26 November that five attacks in recent days used AI agents, frameworks that find weaknesses, pick tools and plan their next steps largely on their own. Four of the five compromised systems. Three targets were critical-infrastructure operators, which public broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers; no port or shipping victim was named. BACS gave no victim names or attribution and has not said whether any control systems were reached. The entry points were ordinary: default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems, the pattern the UK NCSC described on 24 November (see below). Editorial assessment: satcom routers, terminal VPNs and fleet portals with default credentials are exactly what these tools find first.

items.title: UK NCSC says AI-assisted attacks are exploiting familiar weaknesses in internet-facing services faster, and urges operators to cut exposure
items.content_text: The UK National Cyber Security Centre said in a 24 November blog post that it has seen a rise since September in AI-assisted, or “agentic”, attacks that exploit long-known weaknesses in internet-facing services, compressing the time between a flaw becoming public and its use against exposed systems. Its advice centres on reducing what is reachable from the internet, patching exposed services quickly and keeping an accurate inventory of what is online. The post makes no maritime-specific finding. It fits this week’s GreyNoise report on an AI-assisted crew breaching Check Point managers (see above) and the run of exploited gateways in Critical Advisories. Editorial assessment: shipboard satcom routers, terminal remote-access gateways and fleet-management portals are the kind of exposed, slow-to-patch services this guidance targets.

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT or maritime victim is reported, but such gateways often front port, terminal and fleet-management networks, and ESXi often hosts terminal-operating and monitoring servers (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT or maritime operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning for port and terminal networks (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group entered through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims are named. Editorial assessment: terminal operating systems and OT monitoring tools often run as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts.

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: Hackers probe 14 newly disclosed flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers, a risk for port cold stores and reefer facilities
items.content_text: VulnCheck has disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO, the Dixell supervisory system used in supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration; each gave its researcher root on test units. Nine affect only firmware built before a 2021 rewrite. The other five reach the latest firmware: the daily admin password is derived from the device’s MAC address and the date, and the MAC address is visible without logging in. VulnCheck saw exploitation attempts against two older-firmware flaws within two hours of the 12 November CVE publication and calls the sources opportunistic scanners. Copeland ended support on 16 March 2026 and will not fix the five current-firmware flaws; nearly 2,000 units are internet-reachable. No port or vessel victim is reported. Editorial assessment: port cold stores and reefer facilities that use these supervisors should treat them as exposed until isolated or replaced.

items.title: Danfoss puts two critical CVEs on the refrigeration managers used in cold stores, with no fix for AK-SM 8xxA until firmware 5.5.x
items.content_text: Danfoss published two advisories on 20 November covering its AK-SM and AK-SC refrigeration system managers, the controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage plants, including cold stores at ports and food-import terminals. CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS v4 9.3) is a stack buffer overflow in an unauthenticated web handler of AK-SM 8xxA units up to and including firmware 5.4.0; the fix comes in the upcoming 5.5.x release. CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS v4 9.9) covers default credentials documented for legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800 units, all versions. CISA republished the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA advisory as ICSA-26-328-03 on 24 November. Neither CVE is reported exploited, but internet-facing refrigeration controllers were the target of this month’s European attacks. Editorial assessment: until 5.5.x ships, removing internet exposure is the real control.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Danfoss advisories and CVEs 20 Nov 2026; CISA republication 24 Nov 2026; fix pending in firmware 5.5.x

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds sector material for maritime vessels
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for maritime vessels alongside water, food and agriculture, freight rail, building automation and cloud-connected industrial IoT. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions and applying zero-trust principles. Regulators, insurers and auditors often use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what ship and terminal operators are asked to show. Editorial assessment: the comment window is the chance to flag guidance that would not work aboard a ship.

items.title: FDD proposes making space systems the 17th US critical-infrastructure sector, citing threats to satellite navigation signals
items.content_text: The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank, published a monograph on 24 November arguing that Congress should designate space-based systems as the 17th US critical-infrastructure sector, with NASA as the lead federal agency for risk management, threat sharing and resilience planning. The authors say the designation would not create a new regulatory regime or displace existing authorities. They cite positioning, navigation and timing services as underpinning shipping, finance and agriculture, and warn that China and Russia are fielding capabilities to jam satellite communications and falsify navigation signals. It is a proposal only; no bill or agency action has followed. Editorial assessment: for ship operators, PNT resilience on the bridge remains an operational planning issue whatever happens to the proposal.

items.title: Marshall Islands flag warns of targeted attacks on shipboard satcom-edge firewalls and VPNs, and tells crews not to reset compromised systems
items.content_text: The Republic of the Marshall Islands Maritime Administrator issued Ship Security Advisory No. 08-26 on 30 October, SAFETY4SEA reported on 4 November. It cites the two US-bound vessels boarded by the US Coast Guard and FBI in August after suspected cyberattacks, one with a communications outage of more than 30 hours but no reported operational disruption. The advisory names firewalls, routers and VPN concentrators at the satellite-communications boundary as the main risk, often third-party managed and on outdated firmware, and references Fortinet FortiGate exploitation. It warns that upgrading firmware alone is not enough because stolen credentials may remain valid, calls for IT/OT separation, and tells crews not to reset, reconfigure or power down affected systems so evidence is kept. Incidents on RMI-flagged vessels must be reported. Editorial assessment: the satcom edge is the ship’s front door.

items.title: ClassNK publishes the second edition of its ship cyber security management guidelines, with audit criteria mapped to RightShip, SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA vetting
items.content_text: Classification society ClassNK announced on 30 October the second edition of its guidelines for cyber security management systems (CSMS) on ships and clarified its certification requirements, Maritime Gateway reported on 3 November. Part 1 sets out the CSMS requirements and Part 2 the audit criteria and the evidence auditors expect. The structure references ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 and covers management commitment, shore and onboard responsibilities, risk assessment, operational controls and incident preparedness, and the audit criteria are mapped to the RightShip (RISQ), OCIMF SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA vetting schemes. The guidelines are separate from IACS unified requirements E26 and E27, which apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. Editorial assessment: tanker and bulk operators facing several vetting regimes can build one evidence set for all of them.
